rows.label: P2
rows.article: The other one shows up when you get close

source.quote: Reactive protection often arrives when pain gets close. You suddenly want to drink, smoke, eat, scroll, text somebody, plan something, fix something, sleep, dissociate, get angry, or act out sexually. The response may be trying to step in because nothing else feels able to hold what is coming up.
source.from: the 2026-10-04 r4 guide, Two Common Protective Patterns

headings: Queue drafts that still fail (not in the article)

rows.label: PGQ-001 · B1
rows.text: Feelings about yourself work the same way. "I feel attracted" or "I feel ashamed" is real as a feeling, but it doesn't settle who you are, or who you love. (If you don't want to be touched, though, say no now and work out what it means later. Same if something might be dangerous right now, or might be a medical warning sign: step away or get checked first.)

source.quote: Preserve the distinction between a thought/sensation/attraction/aversion being real as an experience and the conclusion drawn from it.

rows.note: Alone 100% Human (71). Not in without B2, or it would say only half of PGQ-001.

rows.label: PGQ-001 · B2 (second try)
rows.text: If it's your orientation or your gender in question, I wouldn't go the other way and write it off as "just an intrusive thought" only because it's unwanted, or because your family wouldn't like it. There's no rush to decide either way, because you'll find it out over time from what you keep noticing with real people and in how you actually live, and that counts for more than any one feeling, however strong it is. Even if somebody tells you otherwise, feeling the opposite tomorrow wouldn't show you the "real you" either.

source.quote: Do not steer sexuality, orientation, or gender identity in either direction, and do not dismiss genuine identity-relevant experience merely because it is confusing, unwanted, or stigmatized.

rows.note: 100% AI alone, both tries (100 words each). Next: fresh writers, not another rewording.

rows.label: PGQ-003 · C2
rows.text: And being yourself with people doesn't mean telling strangers everything. Privacy isn't fakery. People can earn more of you by how they handle the smaller things you tell them, and how they take it when you say no. But if a relationship is getting deep and you're still keeping up a fake normal, happy version of yourself to hold onto it, I'd either bring more of the truth in, carefully, or let it be less deep for now. (If telling could put you in real danger, like violence, or being outed where that isn't safe, protect yourself first.) And when someone finally accepts you, it can feel amazing. It still doesn't prove they love you, or that they've earned your trust yet.

source.quote: privacy is not fakery; total disclosure is not required. Let people earn deeper access through demonstrated handling of smaller truths, boundaries, and vulnerability.

rows.note: Alone 100% Human (129). Next to C1 the h2 was 16% AI (a 312-word window from the paragraph before C1 through this one), so it waits for another spot.

rows.label: PGQ-004 · F (second try)
rows.text: Anxiety deserves the same kind of listening, but it isn't a fortune teller. It might really be warning you about something, like being overloaded, or a boundary. Most of the time, I'd ask it what it's trying to protect, and then check what it predicted against what actually happens, unless you're really in danger, or it's something in your body like chest pain, which a doctor should look at instead of you waiting to see if the anxiety was right. And when a part of you says no to going deeper, or to an altered state, that no isn't a prediction at all, and it's reason enough to stop. With touch or sex, even a hesitation is enough, and it might not sound like a no at all, more like a part of you going quiet or pulling back a little.

source.quote: Preserve the distinction between protective intent and predictive accuracy.
